hook: An engineer reading a vibration signal wants to know where it is zero and whether it passes through zero or just grazes it. For polynomial functions, the factors answer both questions: each factor gives a zero, and its power says whether the graph crosses or touches. Some zeros are not even real, but they still count.

figure.caption: $p(x) = 0.25(x + 2)(x - 1)^2(x - 3)$ crosses the $x$-axis at the zeros of odd multiplicity, $-2$ and $3$, and touches it at the zero of even multiplicity, $1$.

chain.cause: $(x - a)^k$ is a factor of $p$ and no higher power is

chain.effect: $p$ keeps its sign near $a$: the graph touches the axis without crossing
it has exactly $n$ complex zeros counting multiplicity, real or not

chain.cause: $p$ has real coefficients and a zero $a + bi$ with $b \ne 0$
chain.effect: its conjugate $a - bi$ is a zero too

ideas: Multiplicity: the power of the factor $(x - a)$. Odd: the graph crosses. Even: it touches (a double zero bounces off the axis).
Degree $n$ means $n$ complex zeros counting multiplicity; non-real ones come in conjugate pairs when the coefficients are real.
Equally spaced inputs with constant $n$th differences fit degree $n$.
Even function: $f(-x) = f(x)$, symmetric about the $y$-axis. Odd function: $f(-x) = -f(x)$, symmetric about the origin.

misconception.wrong: A polynomial of degree $4$ always has $4$ $x$-intercepts.
misconception.right: It has $4$ complex zeros counting multiplicity, but some may repeat and some may be non-real. $p$ in the stimulus has degree $4$ and only $3$ $x$-intercepts, because $-1$ counts twice.

summary: Each factor $(x - a)^k$ of a polynomial gives a zero $a$ of multiplicity $k$: the graph crosses at odd multiplicity and touches at even multiplicity. A polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ complex zeros counting multiplicity, and with real coefficients the non-real ones come in conjugate pairs. Constant $n$th differences point to degree $n$; even and odd functions show mirror symmetry.
